Replying to @naomi when pricing my pieces I consider time spent making/decorating/signing/waxing/glazing/sanding/lustering/firing/invetorying. I have done time studies to help gauge the time I spend on making the pieces. I also consider materials used. I apply gold luster to almost every piece and it’s expensive and requires an additional firing which is also another expense. I also consider experience. I have been working with clay for 14 years now so I consider all of those years of working to this point in my pieces value as well. Pricing is hard! Placing a value on your art is uncomfortable. I’m just happy to be here and I’m doing my best with the knowledge I have gained so far on this journey. I don’t think there is a right answer that will work for everyone, I’m just trying to do what feels right to me! Thank you for reading! 💗💗💗💗 #wheelthrown #ceramics #sliptrailing #potterytiktok #porcelain

This artist combines pottery with one of the oldest principles behind animation. Around the rotating part of the ceramic piece, the bird is painted in a sequence of slightly different positions. When it spins fast enough, our eyes no longer perceive each image separately, and the brain connects them into continuous movement, making the bird appear to fly. The effect is similar to early animation devices such as the zoetrope and relies on apparent motion, the same basic idea that allows a rapid sequence of still images to look like moving video. I’m a sucker for the making of pots, the joyous throwing and trimming, but what comes after, the waxing, glazing and firing, is more of a laborious task that normally ends up being highly repetitive. I don’t mind the work, I keep my headphones on and listen to stories throughout the day, yet I definitely experience more pain in my hands from these processes, as compared to throwing and trimming. Specifically, it’s the grasping of pots as I fettle the surface clean, as the fingers that are gripped so tightly around the object cannot move, otherwise they rub down the surface and create thin patches that show in the finished pots. This means that the hand that holds the pots is tensed for hours on end with my fingers pressed against a relatively powdery surface, if I squeeze too hard, the clay can fracture and come off of the vessel and too loose a grip means my digits glide across the surface, again creating thin spots. It’s hard to describe, but essentially this hand becomes a vice whilst the other carefully cleans the surface. It’s a skill, just like any other in the making process. #pottery #glazing #glaze #howto #craftsmanship #ceramics
